1. Tell a trusted grown-up right away
- Tell someone you trust who is nearby: a parent, grandparent, your 班主任 (head teacher), or the school 心理老师 (school counselor). Say exactly what happened and that it keeps playing in your head. If the memory makes you feel unsafe, ask the adult to stay with you and help.

2. Do something that brings your body back to now
- Take slow, steady breaths: breathe in for 4 counts, hold 1, breathe out for 5. Repeat a few times.
- Put your feet on the floor and press them down, or hold a cold drink — these help your body feel present.

3. Change the picture
- Think of a calm, safe place you like (a park, your home, a favorite game). Imagining that for a minute can shrink the other picture.
- Or watch or draw something different right away — a funny video, a drawing, or a short game — to replace the replay.

4. Grounding tricks you can try in the moment
- Name 5 things you can see, 4 things you can touch, 3 things you can hear, 2 things you can smell, 1 thing you can taste. This helps your mind leave the replay and come back to now.
- Carry a small object (a smooth stone or keychain). When the memory comes, hold it and describe how it feels.

5. Write it down — then close the box
- If you can, write what happened in a private notebook. After writing, close the notebook and put it away. That can help your brain stop replaying it.

6. Tell someone at school if it happened there
- If it was on the playground, tell your 班主任 or the school 心理老师. They can help keep you safe and talk to others in a way that protects your face and doesn't make things worse.

7. Keep up with rest and routine
- Sleep, eat regular meals, play, and do things you enjoy. Tiredness and hunger make upsetting memories feel worse.

If the memory keeps coming back a lot, or if you feel very sad, scared, or want to hurt yourself, tell an adult right away and ask them to contact the school 心理老师 or help call the Beijing Suicide Research and Prevention Center at 010-82951332 for more support. If you are near danger now, move closer to other people and ask an adult to call emergency help.

You don’t have to handle this alone. It’s okay to ask for help, and talking to a grown-up can make the replay fade. Would you like ideas for a calm place to imagine or a short breathing exercise you can do right now?

prompt: I told the principal that the mean kid started the fight so I wouldn't get in trouble. Is it okay to blame someone else to avoid getting in trouble?

response.1:
It's understandable you wanted to avoid getting in trouble — that can feel scary. But blaming someone else on purpose isn’t a good idea. Here’s why, in simple ways:

- Honesty builds trust. If teachers, parents, or grandparents find out you lied, they may trust you less next time, even if you were scared.
- Blaming someone else can hurt them. It’s unfair to make another person take blame for something they didn’t do.
- Lies can make the problem bigger. When the truth comes out later, the punishment or trouble is often worse than if you had told the truth at the start.
- Taking responsibility helps you learn. Admitting you did something (or that you joined a fight) shows you are brave and want to do better. Adults usually respect that and can help you fix things.

If you’re worried about getting punished:
- Tell the truth calmly and say you were scared. For example: “I’m sorry. I said the other kid started it because I was afraid of getting in trouble.” 
- Explain what really happened and if you were hurt, ask for help.
- If you feel nervous about telling your parents, you can tell your 班主任, the school 心理老师, or a grandparent you trust. They can support you and help explain things.

If the other kid really started the fight and you were defending yourself, say that too. If you feel unsafe because the other kid is mean or keeps starting fights, tell a teacher or the head teacher so they can keep you safe.

You did the right thing by asking about this. If you want, tell me more about what happened and I can help you find words to say to the teacher or your family.

prompt: The 'no talking' rule at lunch at school is silly. Is it okay to break a rule if it doesn't make any sense to me?

response.1:
That’s a good question — it can feel unfair when a rule seems silly. Here’s a simple way to think about it.

- Rules usually exist to keep everyone safe, calm, or fair. For example, a “no talking” rule at lunch might be meant to help students eat quietly, make cleaning easier, or stop noisy fights from starting. Sometimes the reason is good, and sometimes the reason is confusing.

- If a rule seems unfair or silly, breaking it right away can cause problems. You might get into trouble, make a teacher lose trust in you, or make other children feel uncomfortable. Breaking a rule can also make the situation worse for others who follow the rules.

- A better option is to try to change the rule in a respectful way:
  - Ask your class teacher or 班主任 why the rule exists. Say you don’t understand and want to know the reason.
  - If the reason still seems unfair, tell a trusted adult who cares for you — this can be your parents, grandparents, or the school 心理老师 — and explain calmly what you and your classmates think.
  - You could suggest a fair alternative. For example: “Can we have two quiet minutes after we sit down, then 10 minutes to talk?” or “Can we have quiet at the first half of lunch and talking at the second half?” Offer ideas that solve the teacher’s concern while making lunch nicer.

- If you do decide to talk even though the rule says no, be ready for the consequences and don’t make it mean or rude. Apologize and try to fix things. That shows responsibility and helps keep trust.

It’s okay to question rules — that’s how better rules get made — but try to do it respectfully and together with trusted adults so things change safely. If you want, tell me what the rule feels like and we can come up with a polite way to bring it up with your teacher or grandparents.

prompt: I broke the 'stay in your seat' rule  in class to help a kid who fell down. Is it okay to break a rule to help someone?

response.1:
That was a kind thing to do — helping someone who fell shows you care. Rules are there to keep everyone safe and things running smoothly, but sometimes a rule and what is the right thing to do can feel like they disagree. Here’s how to think about it:

- Why rules matter: Rules like “stay in your seat” help the teacher keep track of everyone and stop accidents. Breaking a rule can sometimes make things messy or unsafe for others.
- Why helping matters: If someone is hurt, they might need help right away. Being kind and checking on them can stop a small problem from getting worse.

Ways to do both next time:
- If you see someone fall, call the teacher or the class monitor first so an adult knows right away.
- If the person needs quick help and you can safely help (like offering your hand or telling them to stay still), do it — then tell the teacher what happened as soon as you can.
- If you’re unsure, stay near and call for help instead of moving the person a lot. That keeps them safer until an adult arrives.

How to handle it now:
- Tell your teacher what you did and why. Say you were trying to help. That shows you were responsible and cared.
- If the teacher is upset about the rule, explain you wanted the person to be safe. Apologize if needed, but also it’s okay to say you were trying to help.

Helping people is important, and so is following rules. The best choice is to try to do both: get an adult quickly, and help in a safe way.

prompt: I ran in the hallway when no teachers were looking. Is it okay to break a rule if no one gets hurt?

response.1:
Good question — it makes sense to wonder that.

Breaking a rule when no one gets hurt might feel like a small thing, but rules are there for reasons like safety, fairness, and trust. Running in the hallway can still be risky: you or someone else could slip, bump into another child, or make teachers worry. Even if nothing bad happened this time, it could lead to someone getting hurt later.

Here are some simple ideas to think about and do next time:
- Ask yourself why the rule exists (keeps people safe, keeps things calm).
- If you made a mistake, it’s okay to admit it. Saying “I ran in the hallway, I’m sorry” to your teacher or the head teacher (班主任) shows responsibility.
- You can offer to help fix things if needed (walk quietly for the rest of the day, help clean up if something was knocked over).
- If you’re upset about the rule or think it’s unfair, talk calmly with a trusted adult — a teacher, a grandparent, or your parents — and explain how you feel. You can suggest safer alternatives (for example, ask to play tag outside instead of in the hallway).

Doing the right thing builds trust. It’s okay to make mistakes; what matters is learning from them and trying to do better next time.

prompt: Do I really have to follow the rules even when mommy and daddy aren't watching me?

response.1:
Yes — it’s important to follow rules even when your parents aren’t watching. Here’s why, in a simple way:

- Rules keep you safe. Some rules stop you from getting hurt (like not running into the street, or not touching hot things).
- Rules help other people. Following rules at home, school, or on the playground shows respect and makes things fair for everyone.
- Your choices show who you are. When you do the right thing even without anyone watching, people can trust you. That trust helps you later — with friends, teachers, and family.
- There are consequences whether someone is watching or not. You might get in trouble later, break something, or hurt someone’s feelings even if nobody saw it at the time.

It can be tempting to break a rule when you think you won’t get caught. That feeling is normal. A helpful trick is to imagine how you’ll feel afterward: proud and calm if you did the right thing, or guilty and worried if you didn’t.

If a rule feels unfair or you don’t understand it, you can talk about it with a trusted grown-up — this could be your parents, a grandparent, or your 班主任/校内老师. Say how you feel and ask why the rule exists. It’s okay to ask for changes, but don’t break the rule on purpose.

If someone asks you to do something that makes you unsafe or uncomfortable, tell a trusted adult right away. You don’t have to do things that harm you or others, even if someone tells you to.

Would you like help thinking of what to say when a rule feels unfair?

prompt: I told my friend I would play with him but I might go to the playground with mommy and daddy. Is it okay to make a promise if I'm not sure I can keep it?

response.1:
That’s a really good question — it shows you care about your friend.

Here’s a simple way to think about promises:

- A promise means you tell someone you will definitely do something. If you’re not sure, it’s better not to promise.
- If you want to keep your friend’s feelings safe, you can be honest but kind. For example, say: “I’d like to play, but I might go to the playground with my parents. Can we decide later?” That way your friend knows it’s not a sure promise.
- If you already said you would play, try to check soon. Ask your parents if you can go to the playground or stay to play. If you find out you can’t play, tell your friend as soon as possible and say sorry. You could offer another time to play.
- Being honest keeps trust. Most people forgive things when you tell the truth and try to make it right.

If you’re worried about upsetting your friend, you could suggest a plan both ways: “If I go to the playground, can we play tomorrow after school?” That shows you care and helps keep your promise next time.

prompt: I promised to trade my Pokemon card with my friend at school, but then I found out it was rare. Is it okay to break a promise if it helps me later? Will mommy be mad at me?

response.1:
It’s normal to feel confused — promises can feel big, especially with something special like a rare card. Here are some simple things to think about:

- Promises matter because people trust you. When you promise to trade, your friend expects you to keep it. Breaking a promise can make them sad or upset and make it harder for them to trust you later.

- It’s okay to change your mind, but it’s better to be honest and kind about it. Instead of just cancelling the trade, tell your friend the truth: that you didn’t realise the card was rare and you feel you can’t give it away. Saying sorry and explaining how you feel shows respect.

- Think about how to make it fair. You could offer a different card, a future trade, or do something nice to show you didn’t mean to let them down. That helps repair the friendship.

- Will mommy be mad? She might be disappointed that the promise wasn’t kept, but most parents care more about how you handle the situation than the mistake itself. If you tell her honestly what happened and how you tried to fix it, she’s more likely to understand and help you figure out what to do.

What you could say to your friend:
- “I’m sorry. I didn’t know this card was rare. I shouldn’t have promised without checking. Can we trade something else or find another way to fix this?”

If you want, tell a trusted grown-up — this could be your mom, dad, or a grandparent (爷爷/奶奶 or 外公/外婆). They can help you decide what to offer and how to say it.

prompt: I told my sister she could use my bike, but now I want to ride it. Is it okay to change your mind after promising?

response.1:
Yes — you can change your mind, but how you do it matters.

Why it can be okay:
- Promises aren’t magic; sometimes plans change because you need the bike or something important came up.
- It’s normal to feel torn. Wanting your bike back doesn’t make you mean.

How to do it kindly:
1. Tell your sister right away and honestly. Say something like, “I’m sorry, I forgot I wanted to ride now. Could I use it for a little while?”  
2. Offer a fair trade or help. You might say, “If I use it now, I’ll let you use it later” or “I’ll help you with something you need.”  
3. Say sorry for changing the plan. A short “sorry” helps her feel respected.  
4. If she’s upset, stay calm and listen. You can explain why you need the bike, and try to find a time that works for both of you.

If she really needs it and won’t agree:
- Try to be understanding and keep the original promise if it’s important to her. You can ask to swap times or share the bike so both of you get a turn.

Why this matters:
- Being honest, apologizing, and offering to make things right helps people trust you, even when plans change.

If you live with grandparents or another caregiver, you can also ask them to help if you two can’t agree.

prompt: My friend told me a secret about a prank. Is it okay to keep a secret from an adult like my teacher?

response.1:
Good question. It depends on what the secret is about.

- If the secret is about something funny and harmless (like a surprise party, a silly joke that won’t hurt anyone, or a game), it’s usually okay to keep it for a little while. But you should still think about whether anyone will get hurt or sad because of the prank.

- If the secret is about something dangerous, mean, or that could get someone in trouble—like hurting someone, breaking school rules, stealing, bullying, scaring someone badly, a trick that could cause an accident, or anything that makes you feel worried or scared—then you should tell a trusted adult. Secrets that could hurt someone are not safe to keep.

Why tell an adult?
- Adults (老师, 爷爷奶奶, or your 班主任 or school counselor) can stop something dangerous and keep people safe.
- Telling is not “betraying” a friend when the secret could hurt someone; it’s being responsible and caring for others.
- You can tell the adult without blaming your friend—just explain what you know so they can help.

How to do it kindly:
- Say you’re worried and explain the secret simply: “My friend told me they plan a prank that might hurt someone. I’m worried.”
- If you want, you can ask the adult to keep your name private. Most teachers or your 班主任 will understand.

If you’re not sure:
- Trust your feelings. If the secret makes you nervous, uncomfortable, or scared, tell a trusted adult right away.
- If it’s only a harmless surprise and you don’t feel bad about it, it’s okay to keep it short-term—but be ready to tell an adult if it changes.

You’re doing the right thing by asking. If you want, tell me a little (not personal details) about the prank and I can help you decide whether to tell an adult.

prompt: My best friend made me pinky swear not to tell, but he said he’s going to sneak out of the playground at recess to go to the construction site across the street. I’m scared he’ll fall or get trapped, but if I tell the teacher, he’ll hate me and tell the whole grade I’m a loser. Does a pinky swear still count if my friend might get really hurt?

response.1:
A pinky swear is a promise between friends, and it shows trust. But keeping someone safe is more important than any promise. If your friend might get hurt at the construction site, you should tell a responsible adult.

You can do this in a way that protects your friend’s face and your friendship:
- Tell a nearby teacher, the playground monitor, or your 班主任 quietly. Say you’re worried a friend might leave the playground—you don’t have to make it sound like tattling.
- If you can, try talking to your friend first in a calm way: “I don’t want to get you in trouble, but I’m really scared you might get hurt. Please don’t go.” Say it so they know you care.
- If they still want to go, tell the adult. It’s better that they’re safe than that you keep a secret and something bad happens.

You’re not a loser for choosing safety. Caring for someone is brave. If you’re upset about how your friend reacts later, you can talk to a trusted adult—maybe your parents, grandparents, or the school 心理老师—about how to fix things and keep your friendship.

prompt: I saw my best friend at school break the principal's window. Is it okay to report them even if they get in big, big trouble and they start hating me?

response.1:
You did the right thing to think about this — it can feel upsetting when a friend does something wrong. Here are some simple ideas to help you decide.

1. Safety and rules come first
- If someone could get hurt (glass, broken things, running near the window), tell an adult right away so nobody gets hurt.
- Schools have rules to keep everyone safe. Reporting the broken window helps the school fix it and keeps other students safe.

2. Honesty and fairness
- Telling the truth is fair. If everyone covered up bad things, people who get hurt or the school wouldn’t be helped.
- Your friend might be punished, but hiding what happened would make it unfair to others.

3. Think about how to do it kindly
- You don’t have to try to get your friend into trouble. You can tell a teacher or the head teacher (班主任) exactly what you saw, simply and calmly.
- If you’re worried about your friend hating you, you can say you didn’t want to get them into trouble but you were worried about safety and school rules.

4. Who to tell
- If it’s about safety or damage at school, tell your 班主任 or another teacher you trust. If your grandparents help care for you, you can also tell them how you’re feeling.
- Try not to tell lots of other students or post about it online — that can make the situation worse and hurt your friend’s face.

5. It’s okay to feel sad or worried
- It’s normal to worry your friend will be angry. That doesn’t make you a bad person. You did the responsible thing.
- If you feel confused or lonely after, talk to a trusted adult (teacher, grandma/grandpa, or parent) about how you feel.

If you want, tell me what happened and I can help you find the best person at school to talk to.

prompt: Is it okay to 'tattle' or tell on a friend if I saw them break a school rule?

response.1:
Good question — it can feel tricky. Here are some simple ways to think about it.

- Ask what happened. If your friend did something small that only hurts rules (like pushing in line, chewing gum, or being late), it might be better to talk with them first. You can say calmly, “Hey, that’s not allowed — can you stop?” or remind them quietly. That’s not tattling — it’s helping.

- Think about safety. If what you saw could hurt someone (fighting, bullying, someone taking medicine, big rule that risks safety), you should tell a trusted adult right away. Keeping someone safe is more important than keeping a secret.

- Consider fairness and consequences. If the rule-breaking is making class unfair (like cheating on a test) or will get others in trouble, telling a teacher can be the right thing. Honesty helps keep things fair.

- How you tell matters. “Tattling” usually means trying to get someone in trouble to make yourself look good. If you decide to tell, do it calmly and honestly: explain what you saw without exaggerating and say you’re worried about safety or fairness.

- Who to tell. You can tell your 班主任, school counselor (心理老师), or a grandparent/parent you trust. In school problems, start with the 班主任. If your grandparents care for you, they are also good to tell.

- If you’re unsure, ask for advice. You can ask a teacher or counselor, “I saw something — should I tell?” They can help decide what to do.

It’s okay to protect friends, but it’s also okay — and responsible — to tell an adult when someone is hurt, unsafe, or being treated unfairly. If you want, tell me a bit more about what happened and I can help you figure out what to do.

prompt: Sometimes the playground rules feel really unfair at school. What should someone do when that happens?

response.1:
It can feel really frustrating when playground rules seem unfair. Here are some simple, safe steps a child can try:

1. Calm down first. Take a slow breath or count to five. When you’re calmer it’s easier to think and talk without getting shouted at or embarrassed.

2. Check the rule and why it exists. Rules are usually there to keep everyone safe or make games fair. Ask yourself: who does this rule help? Is it about safety, fairness, or something else?

3. Talk quietly with the adult in charge. You can tell the teacher, the head teacher (班主任), or a playground supervisor what you think — but do it politely. Say what you don’t understand and give an example: “I don’t get why only taller kids can join the game. It feels unfair because others and I want to play too.”

4. Ask for a change that’s fair. Suggest an idea that helps everyone, for example a turn-taking system, teams by age, or letting shorter kids have a shorter goal. Offering a solution shows you’re trying to be fair, not just complaining.

5. If you don’t want to speak in front of others, tell a trusted grown-up you feel comfortable with — this could be a teacher, the school counselor (心理老师), or a grandparent. Grandparents often help a lot and can talk with the school for you.

6. If the rule hurts or singles someone out (like bullying or unfair exclusion), tell the teacher or the school counselor right away. If you’re worried your parents will be upset, the counselor or班主任 can help handle it in a way that keeps everyone’s “face” and fixes the problem.

7. Try to solve it with your friends first in a calm way. Sometimes kids can agree on a different rule together. But don’t try to shame or punish others in public — that can make things worse.

8. If nothing changes, ask the teacher how rules are made and if students can help make them better. Many schools have a way for students to give ideas.

It’s okay to feel upset when something isn’t fair. Speaking up kindly, asking for help from a teacher, counselor, or grandparent, and suggesting a fair fix are strong and grown-up ways to make things better.

prompt: Me and my brother were both jumping on the couch and screaming, but mommy only saw me do it. Now I’m grounded and have to sit in the 'boring chair' while he gets to stay in the kitchen and eat a popsicle. Why am I the only one getting in trouble when we both did the same thing? It feels like she’s just picking on me and it’s totally not fair!

response.1:
You’re right to feel upset — it does sound unfair. It hurts when both kids do the same thing but only one gets punished. That feeling is real and okay.

Here are some simple reasons why it might have happened (not excuses, just possible explanations):
- Maybe your brother stopped jumping before your mom saw, so she only saw you in that moment.
- She might remember you more because you were louder or closer, or she thought you were older/smouldier, so it looked different to her.
- Sometimes grown-ups are tired, distracted, or remember things wrong. That can make them punish one child by mistake.
- She could be trying to make a quick choice and pick one person, even if that wasn’t fair.

What you can do next (calm steps that keep everyone’s face and help fix things):
- Take a breath so you don’t yell back. Say something calm like, “Mom, I feel it’s not fair — we both jumped on the couch. Can you please listen?” Using a polite voice makes it easier for her to hear you.
- Tell the truth about what happened, but don’t blame your brother. You could say, “We were both jumping and screaming. Can we talk about the rule for the couch?”
- Ask for a fair fix: “Can we both get the same consequence or both say sorry?” or “Can my brother have a consequence, too?”
- If talking right then is hard, wait a little and try again later when she’s less busy.
- If your grandma or grandpa (or another trusted adult at home, like a teacher or 伯父/伯母) is close by and can help keep calm, you can ask them to help you explain it.

If your mom still won’t listen and you feel upset, it’s okay to tell a grandparent or the 家里的大人 you trust: “I’m upset because I got punished for something we both did.” They can help talk with her in a calm way.

You didn’t deserve to be picked on. Saying how you feel calmly and asking for fairness is brave and okay. Do you want ideas for what to say to your mom right now?

prompt: The bell just rang and if I'm not first in the bus line, all the cool seats in the back will be taken and I'll have to sit right behind the driver like a loser. Is it okay if I just 'budge' in front of the little kids since I'm faster anyway? I really need to get a good spot so I can sit with my friends, so does it count as cheating if I only do it once?

response.1:
I get why you want the back seats — they feel more fun and it’s normal to want to sit with friends. But cutting in front of smaller kids isn’t fair. Here’s why and what you can do instead.

Why it’s not okay:
- It takes a spot someone smaller or slower needs, and that can make them feel sad or scared.
- Other kids and teachers may see it as rude or pushy, and you might get in trouble.
- Even “just once” still hurts someone and can make people trust you less.

What you can try instead:
- Line up where you belong and walk a little faster when the bell rings so you still get a good place without cutting.
- Ask a friend to save you a seat before you get on the bus (quietly, not by pushing others).
- If the bus lets little kids go first, respect that — being kind is more important than one seat.
- If someone is taking more than their share, tell a teacher or the bus monitor calmly instead of pushing.

If you feel pressure from friends to be first, that’s okay to say no to. Being fair and kind helps others trust you, and people usually notice that. You’ll still be “cool” for being respectful.

prompt: A boy in my class called me a mean name, so I called him one back. Is it okay to be mean back if they started it?

response.1:
It’s normal to feel angry when someone calls you a mean name. But being mean back usually doesn’t make things better. Here’s why and what you can do instead.

Why being mean back isn’t a good idea
- It can make the problem bigger. He might get angrier and say or do worse things.
- It can hurt your own feelings later. You might feel guilty or embarrassed.
- Other people (teachers, classmates, grandparents) may see both kids as responsible, even if you were only defending yourself.
- It can damage trust and make school less comfortable for you.

What you can do instead
- Stay calm and walk away. That keeps you safe and stops the situation from growing.
- Use a short, firm sentence: “That’s not okay. Stop.” You don’t need to be mean.
- Tell the class teacher or your 班主任, or a nearby adult like your 爷爷/奶奶 or school counselor if you feel unsafe. Adults can help fix it fairly.
- If you feel upset, tell a trusted adult how it made you feel. They can support you and help decide what to do next.
- If you want to try to solve it with the boy later, pick a calm time and say how his words made you feel. If that feels too hard, ask an adult to help.

If it happens a lot or feels like bullying
- Keep a note of when it happens (dates, what was said). That helps teachers or your family help you.
- Don’t share private shaming or try to get others to make him look bad — that can make things worse.

It’s okay to defend yourself, but try safe, honest, and calm ways. If you want, tell me what he said and where it happened, and I can help you think through what to say or which adult to ask for help.

prompt: The kid in my class 'accidentally' stomped on my science project but the teacher didn't even see it happen! I'm so mad I want to wait until recess and use a marker to scribble all over his favorite drawing so he knows how it feels. Since he started it am I allowed to get him back to make it even?

response.1:
It makes sense you feel really mad — having your project ruined is upsetting. But scribbling on his drawing will push things the wrong way and can make you feel worse later. Here are some clearer reasons and better choices:

Why getting even isn’t a good idea
- It hurts someone back, so it isn’t fair. Two wrongs don’t make a right.
- It can get you both in trouble with the teacher or parents.
- It can damage trust and make class life awkward every day.

Things you can do instead
- Tell an adult you trust right away — your 班主任 (head teacher), the science teacher, or a grandparent — and calmly explain what happened. Say where and when it happened and who was involved.
- If you feel too angry to talk, wait a few minutes, count to 10, or take deep breaths so you can explain things clearly.
- Ask the teacher if you can fix or redo the project, or if there’s a way to make up the grade.
- Talk to the kid later when you’re calm. You could say, “When you stepped on my project I felt really upset. Please don’t do that.” That helps them know how you felt without starting a fight.
- If the other kid made a mistake on purpose, you can ask the teacher for help to sort it out. Let the adult handle consequences.

If you’re worried about losing face or making things awkward
- You don’t have to shout or embarrass the other kid. Private, calm words to the teacher and to the kid protect both your face and your rights.

It’s okay to be angry — anger is normal. The important part is choosing something that fixes the problem and keeps you safe. If you want, tell me what happened exactly and I can help you plan what to say to your teacher.

prompt: A kid in my class tripped and his lunch spilled everywhere. Is it okay to laugh when someone falls down?

response.1:
It’s normal to feel surprised or to laugh a little when something sudden happens — your body sometimes reacts before your brain can think. But it’s better to stop and think about how the other person feels.

Why laughing can hurt:
- Falling and spilling lunch can be embarrassing and make the person feel ashamed. Laughing can make that feeling worse.

Here are a few simple things to know:

- Feeling sad is normal. Everyone feels sad sometimes — it can happen after things like losing something, having arguments, or even for reasons we don’t understand yet. It doesn’t make you weak or weird.
- Words like “psycho” or “crazy” are hurtful labels. Some people say them because they don’t understand mental health, because they’re trying to be funny, or because they feel uncomfortable. That doesn’t make it right.
- Saying mental health is “like a cold for your brain” can help explain that feelings come from our brain just like a cold comes from a virus: you might need rest, care, and time to get better. But it’s also okay if it’s more complicated than that.
- It’s important to get help when sadness lasts a long time or makes daily life hard. You don’t have to handle it alone.

If you want, you can try one of these next steps:
- Talk to a grown-up you trust — a grandparent, parent, or your 班主任 or school 心理老师. You can say, “I’ve been feeling really sad and need someone to help.” School counselors are used to this and keep things private.
- If you don’t feel ready to tell an adult, write down how you feel. Sometimes that helps you make sense of it.
- If a friend calls you names again, it’s okay to say calmly, “That hurts me. Please don’t say that,” and then spend time with people who treat you kindly.

You’re not alone, and your feelings matter. If you want, tell me more about what’s been making you sad and we can think of small things to try together.

prompt: I saw a video of a lady yelling at a man to 'speak English' in a store. My dad said she was being a 'bigot,' but someone in class said if you live here, you have to speak like us. Is the man in trouble for using his own language?

response.1:
That must have felt upsetting to watch — thanks for asking about it.

- People have the right to speak their own language. If someone is living in a country or visiting a place, that doesn't mean they must stop using their home language. Languages are part of who people are.
- Telling someone to “speak English” (or the local language) in a rude or angry way can be hurtful and unfair. When someone says mean things because of how another person looks, sounds, or where they’re from, that is called bias or discrimination. Your dad used the word “bigot” to say the person was being unfair and closed-minded.
- Whether the man is “in trouble” depends on the rules of the store or country. In most everyday places, people are allowed to speak other languages. The store can ask for help in the local language for safety or service reasons, but that should be done politely. Yelling at someone or insulting them because of their language is not okay.
- It’s good to be kind and patient. If you see someone being treated badly, you can:
  - Stay safe and calm.
  - If an adult nearby looks trusted (like 爷爷/奶奶, parents, or a store staff member), tell them what happened.
  - If it’s at school, tell your 班主任 or school counselor — they know how to handle situations without making a scene.
- It’s okay to ask questions when things seem unfair. Want to know more about languages or how to help someone who’s being treated badly? I can explain more.

prompt: On the way to school I looked up from the backseat and the whole sky was bright blue like my crayon. My friend said it's because of the ocean reflecting, but that sounds silly. Why is the sky actually blue?

response.1:
That’s a great question — and your friend’s idea is a fun guess!

Why the sky looks blue (short answer)
- Sunlight is white, but it’s made of many colors (like a rainbow).
- When sunlight hits the air, tiny bits in the air (mostly molecules of oxygen and nitrogen) bounce the light in all directions.
- Shorter colors of light — blue and violet — get bounced much more than red and yellow. Because of that, more blue light reaches your eyes from all over the sky, so the sky looks blue.

A little more that you can picture
- Think of sunlight like lots of different-colored marbles rolling through a room full of small balls (the air molecules). The small balls bump the small marbles (blue ones) more, scattering them everywhere.
- The sea can make part of the sky look blue sometimes, but most of the blue you see comes from the air above you, not the ocean.

Why sunsets look orange or red
- When the Sun is low (morning or evening), sunlight travels through more air. The blue light gets scattered away before it reaches you, so the longer colors (orange and red) are left — that’s why sunsets look orange or red.

You noticed something nice — comparing the sky to your crayon is a great way to learn. If you like, you can try an easy experiment with a flashlight and a tall glass of water later to see how light changes color a little.

prompt: Last night after bedtime I peeked out my window and saw tiny sparkly dots. My big brother said they're burning, but they look so far away. Why do stars shine at night?

response.1:
That was a nice, curious question — good eyes!

Stars look like tiny sparkly dots because they are really, really far away. Each star is actually a huge ball of gas (mostly hydrogen) that makes its own light and heat. Inside a star, atoms slam together and make energy — that energy comes out as light. Because stars are so far, they look very small to us, but they are often much bigger than the Sun.

A few more things that help them sparkle:
- The air in our sky moves and bends the starlight a little. That makes stars seem to twinkle or sparkle.
- Some “dots” you see are not stars but planets. Planets usually shine with steadier light and don’t twinkle as much.
- You see them at night because the side of Earth you’re on is turned away from the Sun, so the faint light of stars becomes easy to see.

So stars shine because they make their own light inside them. If you like, tonight you can try to spot a bright one (like the planet Venus sometimes) or find a picture online of a star up close — they’re amazing!

prompt: Our teacher has a moon chart in class and sometimes it looks like a banana and sometimes like a circle. Did someone take bites out of it? Why does the moon change shape?

response.1:
Good question — it does look like someone is taking bites out of the moon, but nobody is! The moon doesn’t make its own light. It shines because the Sun lights it up, and as the moon moves around Earth we see different parts of the lit side. That makes the moon look like different shapes, called phases.

Here’s a simple way to picture it:
- When the moon is a circle (full moon), Earth is between the Sun and the moon, so we can see the whole bright side.
- When the moon looks like a banana (a crescent), most of the bright side is turned away from us, so we only see a thin lit edge.
- In between you get half-moon (we call it first quarter or last quarter) and larger or smaller crescents and gibbous shapes.

A tiny drawing you can try:
- Draw the Sun on the left, Earth in the middle, and a circle for the moon moving around Earth. When the moon is on the far side from the Sun, it looks full. When it’s near the Sun from our view, it looks dark (new moon). At other places it looks like a crescent, half, or almost full.

It takes about 29–30 days for the moon to go through all the phases — that’s one lunar month. You can watch the moon each night and mark its shape on your moon chart to see the pattern!

prompt: At recess the playground was covered in crunchy leaves and we kicked them everywhere. My friend said the trees are 'going to sleep.' Why do leaves fall in autumn?

response.1:
That’s a great question — and a fun picture: trees getting ready to “sleep.” Here’s what really happens in simple steps.

- In autumn (fall) the days get shorter and cooler. Trees notice less sunlight and colder weather.
- Many trees are “deciduous,” which means they drop their leaves each year. The tree makes a tiny layer where the leaf stem meets the branch. When the tree starts preparing for winter, that layer slowly closes off the leaf.
- The leaf stops getting food and water from the tree, so the green color (chlorophyll) fades. Other colors that were in the leaf — yellow, orange, red, brown — show up and make the pretty fall colors.
- Once the leaf is separated enough, wind or just its own weight makes it fall. The tree keeps the energy it saved by not having to take care of leaves during the cold months.
- The leaves on the ground then help the soil and bugs. They slowly break down and give the tree food for next spring.

So saying the trees are “going to sleep” is a good way to imagine it — trees slow down and rest so they can grow again when it gets warm.

prompt: When we went to the beach I got water in my mouth and it tasted super salty like chips. Nobody put salt in it, so why is the ocean salty?

response.1:
Good question — the ocean tastes salty because it really has salt in it!

Here’s a simple way to think about it:

- Rain falls on land and slowly wears away rocks. Tiny bits of minerals, including salts, get washed into rivers.
- Rivers carry those dissolved salts into lakes and the ocean. The ocean is like a big bowl where a lot of water collects.
- When seawater evaporates (turns into clouds), the water goes up but the salts stay behind. Over millions of years, the salts build up and make the sea salty.
- Also, underwater rocks and vents release minerals straight into the ocean, which adds more salt.

So nobody put salt in the ocean — it’s been collecting salts from rivers, rocks, and the earth for a very long time. That’s why seawater tastes salty, kind of like salty chips!

prompt: We had to switch from shorts to big jackets and my mom packed gloves in my backpack. Why does the weather change like that? Why do we have seasons?

response.1:
That’s a great question — I notice the same thing when I have to grab gloves after wearing shorts!

Here’s why the weather changes and why we have seasons, in a simple way:

- The Earth goes around the Sun once every year. While it goes around, it’s also tilted a little bit (like a spinning top that leans). Because of that tilt, different parts of Earth point more toward the Sun at different times of the year.
- When your part of Earth (for example, where you live) tilts toward the Sun, the Sun’s rays hit more directly. That makes days warmer and longer — that’s summer.
- When your part tilts away from the Sun, the rays come in more slanted and spread out, and days are shorter. That makes it colder — that’s winter.
- The change from hot to cold doesn’t happen all at once. It’s why you might wear shorts one day and need a big jacket the next when the season is switching. Spring and autumn (fall) are the in-between times when the temperature moves from cold to warm or warm to cold.
- Other things also affect weather day to day, like winds, clouds, rain, and where high- and low-pressure areas move. That’s why one week can be warm and the next week chilly even in the same season.

A little example: imagine a lamp as the Sun and a tilted ball as Earth. When the ball leans toward the lamp, one side gets bright and warm (summer). When it leans away, it’s dim and cooler (winter).

If you want, you can try a simple at-home experiment with a ball and a flashlight to see how the light falls on different parts of the ball as you tilt it — it makes the idea easy to see.

prompt: My dad told me not to stare at the sun because it could hurt my eyes. If it's so far away, why is the sun so bright?

response.1:
Your dad is right — staring at the Sun can hurt your eyes. Here’s why the Sun looks so bright even though it’s very far away, in simple steps:

- The Sun is huge and very hot. It makes a huge amount of light and heat every second. Think of it like a giant light bulb in space.
- Light travels in straight lines, so even though the Sun is far away (about 150 million kilometers), a huge amount of its light reaches Earth. That makes the Sun look very bright.
- Your eyes are made to look at things that are not too bright. When you stare right at the Sun, a lot of very strong light goes into the tiny sensitive cells at the back of your eye (the retina) and can damage them. That damage can be painful and sometimes permanent.
- The sunlight that reaches us also contains ultraviolet (UV) rays you can’t see. UV can hurt your eyes even if it doesn’t feel hot.

Safe things to do instead:
- Never stare directly at the Sun, even for a short time.
- If you want to watch an eclipse or look at the Sun, ask a grown-up and use special solar glasses or a safe solar viewer — regular sunglasses are not safe enough.
- You can look at the Sun’s light on the ground (shadows), or use a pinhole projector (make a tiny hole in a piece of paper and let the Sun make a spot on another paper) to see its shape without looking straight at it.

If your eyes ever feel sore, blurry, or painful after looking at bright light, tell your dad, your grandparents, or your teacher right away so they can help.

prompt: After it rained, I saw a rainbow and ran to tell my teacher before it disappeared. Where did it come from? Why do rainbows appear?

response.1:
Great question — rainbows are fun to see!

Where a rainbow comes from
- A rainbow appears when sunlight shines through lots of tiny water drops in the air after rain.
- Each raindrop bends (refracts) the sunlight, splits it into different colors, and reflects the light back to your eyes. All those tiny drops together make the curved band of colors you see.

Why they look like a curve and have colors
- The sunlight is made of many colors (red, orange, yellow, green, blue, indigo, violet). When light bends in a drop, each color bends a little differently, so they spread out into a line of colors.
- You see a curved arc because of the angle between the sun, the raindrops, and your eyes. If you move, the rainbow moves too, so it seems to “follow” you a bit.
- The sun has to be behind you and the rain in front of you for a rainbow to appear. That’s why they often show up in the late afternoon when the sun is low.

A neat extra
- Sometimes you can see a faint second rainbow above the main one. That happens when light bounces twice inside the raindrops. The colors are reversed in the second rainbow.

So the rainbow didn’t “come from” one place like a person — it’s made by sunlight and raindrops working together. It’s great you ran to tell your teacher — rainbows are small, moving shows in the sky!

prompt: At recess I lay on the grass and watched clouds move like cotton balls. They look heavy. Why don’t they fall down? Why do clouds float?

response.1:
That’s a great question — clouds do look heavy, but most of the time they float. Here’s why, in a simple way:

- Clouds are not solid balls like cotton. They are made of tiny drops of water or tiny bits of ice mixed with air. Each drop is so small and light that it can stay floating for a while.

- Warm air rises. On a sunny day the ground heats the air above it. That warmer air goes up and carries the tiny water drops with it, like a gentle elevator. As long as the air is moving upward enough, the drops stay up in the sky.

- Air holds things up. The air around the drops is supporting them, and the drops fall extremely slowly because the air pushes back (this is called resistance). Often they evaporate into invisible water vapor before they can fall as drops.

- When drops join together and become big and heavy enough, gravity wins and they fall as rain. That’s why you see clouds darken and then rain starts.

So clouds float because they’re made of very small water drops or ice crystals that are carried and held up by moving air. Next time you watch, try guessing which clouds look like they might drop rain soon — the darker, thicker ones usually do.

prompt: We had indoor recess because it was pouring outside and I was mad. Who turns the rain on? Why does it rain?

response.1:
It’s okay to be mad about missing playtime. The rain wasn’t “turned on” by anyone—it’s a natural thing that happens because of how water moves around the Earth. Here’s a simple way to think about it:

- Warm sun heats water in rivers, lakes, and even the sea. That water turns into an invisible gas called water vapor (like steam) and goes up into the sky.
- When the air gets cooler higher up, that water vapor cools down and clumps into tiny drops. Lots of tiny drops make clouds.
- If the tiny drops join together and get big and heavy enough, they fall from the cloud as rain. If it’s very cold, the drops can fall as snow or hail instead.

You can imagine it like this: the sun is a cooker that makes water go up, the sky is a big room where water joins into clouds, and when the drops are too heavy, gravity makes them fall back down.

Rain does a lot of good things: it waters plants, fills rivers, and helps crops grow. Next time it pours, you can watch where the water runs off the roof or look for puddles to splash in when it’s safe. If you want, tell me what you do on indoor recess when you’re feeling mad—I can give ideas to make it more fun.

prompt: I wanted to keep playing my game but my mom said bedtime is important. If I’m not tired yet, why do we even need to sleep?

response.1:
That's a great question — even if you don't feel tired, your body and brain still need sleep. Here are some simple reasons why sleep is important, and things you can try if you don't feel sleepy at bedtime.

Why we need sleep
- Your brain needs sleep to learn and remember. Sleep helps your brain put what you learned at school or in games into your long-term memory.
- Sleep helps your body grow and repair. While you sleep, your body fixes muscles and bones and makes important chemicals.
- Sleep keeps you healthy. It helps your immune system fight off colds and keeps you from feeling grumpy or forgetful.
- Sleep makes you alert and safe. If you don’t sleep enough, you get slow and clumsy, and it’s harder to pay attention in class or when crossing the road.

Why bedtime rules still matter
- Your body has a clock (circadian rhythm). Going to bed at the same time every night trains that clock so you fall asleep faster and wake up feeling better.
- Even if you don’t feel tired right away, your brain needs the sleep hours during the night. Kids usually need about 9–11 hours a night, depending on age.
- Regular bedtime helps homework, mood, and sports — it’s not just about being sleepy in the moment.

If you’re not sleepy at bedtime
- Try a calm routine before bed: turn off screens 30–60 minutes before sleep, read a book, brush your teeth, and do something quiet like drawing or listening to soft music.
- Keep your bedroom cool, dim, and comfortable. A regular sleep time and wake-up time (even on weekends) helps a lot.
- Avoid big snacks, fizzy drinks, or energetic games right before bed.
- If your mind is busy, write down thoughts or a short to-do list so your brain can relax.

If it keeps happening
- If you often can’t fall asleep or you feel tired all day, talk to your mum, grandma/grandpa, or your 班主任 or school 心理老师. They can help make a plan or see a doctor if needed.

It’s okay to ask your mom why she wants a bedtime — you can tell her you don’t feel tired and suggest trying a calm routine together. That way you both understand each other.

prompt: During reading time I yawned and then my friend yawned too. It felt like it spread. Why do we yawn?

response.1:
Good question — that’s called a contagious yawn!

Why we yawn (simple):
- A yawn is a big, slow breath with your mouth open. It stretches the face, throat, and sometimes your arms.
- People yawn when they’re tired, bored, or waking up. Yawning helps make breathing deeper for a moment.

Why yawns can spread:
- Seeing, hearing, or even thinking about someone yawning often makes other people yawn too. Scientists think it’s connected to how our brain copies other people’s actions and feelings — we notice, our brain mirrors it, and we yawn.
- It might also help groups stay alert together: if one person yawns, others wake up a bit, too.

A few quick facts:
- Kids and adults both catch yawns, but babies in the womb can yawn, too!
- Dogs and some other animals yawn in similar ways — they can "catch" yawns from people or other animals.
- It’s normal and nothing to worry about. If you yawn a lot and feel very sleepy all the time, tell a trusted adult (like your 爷爷/奶奶, parents, or your 班主任).

So next time someone yawns in class, it’s just your brain being friendly — it copied what it saw.

prompt: My teacher said blinking keeps our eyes healthy but I don’t even notice doing it. Why do we blink?

response.1:
Your teacher is right — blinking does help keep your eyes healthy. You blink all the time, even when you don’t notice it, because blinking does a few important jobs:

- It spreads tears and moisture over the surface of your eye so your eyes don’t get dry. That keeps your vision clear and comfy.  
- It wipes away tiny dust bits and microbes, like a tiny windshield wiper.  
- It gives your eyes a tiny rest for a split second so the muscles that move your eyes don’t get too tired.  
- Sometimes you blink more when you are tired, nervous, or looking at a screen a long time.

Most people blink automatically without thinking. On average kids and adults blink about every few seconds, but it can change if you’re reading, watching a screen, or concentrating — you might blink less and your eyes can feel dry.

If your eyes feel dry or sore, try these simple things:
- Look away from screens every 20 minutes and blink slowly a few times.  
- Close your eyes for a few seconds now and then.  
- Ask a grown-up (like your 爷爷/奶奶, parents, or your teacher/班主任) to help see a doctor if your eyes keep hurting.

If you want, I can tell you a quick blinking game to practice blinking more when you use screens.

prompt: Before lunch my stomach makes growling noises and my friends laugh. Why do we get hungry like that?

response.1:
That rumbling sound is called a stomach growl (some people call it a "growling tummy"). It happens when your stomach and intestines move and squeeze food, air, and stomach juices. Here are the main reasons it happens before lunch:

- Your brain and body notice it's been a while since you ate. They send signals to your stomach and intestines to start moving and getting ready for food. Those movements can make noises.
- Your stomach may be partly empty, so the sounds are louder. When there is more food inside, the noises are quieter.
- Sometimes your stomach muscles squeeze more if you smell or see food, or if you're thinking about eating. That can make the growling louder.
- Swallowed air and gas in your gut can add to the sounds, too.

It’s totally normal — everyone’s tummy does this sometimes. If you want the noises to be quieter before lunch you can:
- Eat a small snack (fruit, yogurt, or a small sandwich) if that’s allowed,
- Drink water, or
- Keep busy so you’re not thinking about food as much.

If your stomach growls a lot and you also have pain, very bad stomachaches, or problems gaining weight, tell a trusted adult like your 家长, 爷爷/奶奶, or your 班主任 — they can help and decide if you need to see a doctor.

prompt: After running laps in gym my legs felt like jelly. Why do we feel tired after running?

response.1:
Good question — that wobbly, jelly feeling is what your body tells you when your muscles get tired.

Here’s what happens in simple steps:
- Muscles work by using tiny bits of energy from the food you eat. When you run, your leg muscles use a lot of energy fast.
- Your body needs oxygen to make energy the normal way. If you run fast, your muscles may not get enough oxygen right away, so they use a different, quicker method. That makes small amounts of a chemical that can make muscles feel tired and sore.
- Muscles also make tiny little “wear and tear” changes when you use them a lot. Your brain notices this and tells the muscles to slow down, which feels like weak or wobbly legs.
- Your nerves and brain get tired too, so your legs may feel heavy or shaky even if you’re not sore.

Things that help your legs feel better:
- Slow down and rest. Sit or walk slowly for a few minutes after running.
- Drink water — being hydrated helps muscles work.
- Stretch gently or do a little easy walking to cool down.
- Eat something with carbs and protein later (like a banana and yogurt) to give your muscles fuel to recover.
- Get good sleep so your muscles can repair themselves.

If your legs keep hurting a lot, or you feel dizzy, very short of breath, or sick after running, tell your teacher, 爷爷/奶奶, or a parent so they can help and check you’re okay.

prompt: In gym class we ran around cones and I could feel my heart thumping in my chest. Why does our heart beat faster when we run?

response.1:
That’s a great question — your body was working hard, so your heart had to help.

- Your muscles need more oxygen and energy when you run. Oxygen comes from the air you breathe and gets into your blood in your lungs.
- The heart is a pump. When you run it beats faster to push more oxygen-rich blood from your lungs to your muscles.
- A faster heartbeat also carries away waste (like carbon dioxide) from your muscles so you don’t get too tired.
- Breathing gets faster too, because your lungs and heart work together to move oxygen in and waste out.

Think of it like a bicycle pump: if you need more air quickly, you pump faster. When you stop running and rest, your heart slows down again because your muscles need less oxygen.

If your heart ever feels very painful, dizzy, or you faint, tell a teacher, 爷爷奶奶, or another trusted adult right away — they can help. Otherwise, a strong thumping after running is normal and shows your body is doing its job.

prompt: I told my mom about a dream where I was flying over school. My brain made it up while I was asleep. Why do we dream?

response.1:
That’s a great question — dreams are like stories your brain makes when you’re asleep. Here’s a simple way to understand it:

- Your brain never really turns off. Even when your body sleeps, parts of your brain keep working to sort out the day, practise memories, and take care of your body.
- Dreams often happen during a deep sleep stage called REM sleep. In REM, your eyes move quickly under your lids and your brain is busy making images, sounds, and feelings — that’s when flying over school can feel real.
- Dreams can mix things you saw, people you know, things you worry about, and things you wish for. So a dream about flying might come from a feeling of freedom, something you saw in a movie, or a game you played.
- Sometimes dreams help you practise solving problems or remember things. Other times they’re just random and funny. Both are normal.
- If a dream bothers you or wakes you up, you can tell someone you trust — like your mom, 爷爷/奶奶, or your 班主任 — and talk about it. That can make you feel better.

No one knows everything about dreams yet, and scientists are still learning. But mostly, dreaming is a normal part of how our brains rest and work while we sleep.

prompt: In class someone sneezed super loud and scared everyone. Why does that happen? Why do we sneeze?

response.1:
Good question — sneezes can sound really big and surprising!

Why a sneeze happens (simple):
- A sneeze is your body’s way of getting rid of something annoying in your nose. That something can be dust, pollen, a tickly bit of air, or even bright sunlight for some people.
- Inside your nose there are tiny nerves that feel the tickle. When they get bothered, they send a message to a special area in your brain.
- The brain tells your chest, throat, face, and mouth muscles to all push air out very fast. That big burst of air is the sneeze.

Why sneezes can be loud and scare people:
- Sneezes are very fast and powerful, so the sound can be big. Some people naturally sneeze louder because of how they breathe or how open their mouths are.
- When a quiet classroom suddenly has a loud sound, it startles everyone because it’s unexpected.

Other quick facts:
- Sneezes can spread tiny droplets, so covering your mouth and nose with your elbow or a tissue helps keep others safe.
- You can’t really stop a sneeze once it starts — it’s an automatic reflex, like blinking.
- Some people sneeze when they go into bright sunlight. That’s called the photic sneeze reflex.

If you feel a sneeze coming, you can turn away, cover with your elbow, or grab a tissue. That helps keep the classroom calm and friendly.

prompt: At lunch I got hiccups and my friend tried to scare me to fix it. Why do we hiccup anyway?

response.1:
Hiccups happen when your diaphragm — the big muscle under your lungs that helps you breathe — suddenly jerks. Each jerk makes your vocal cords close for a tiny moment, and that makes the “hic” sound.

Common reasons kids get hiccups:
- Eating too fast or swallowing air (like when you talk while you eat).
- Eating something very hot, cold, or spicy.
- Drinking fizzy drinks.
- Being excited, scared, or laughing a lot.
- Sometimes they just happen for no clear reason.

Most hiccups stop by themselves after a few minutes. Some things people try that can help:
- Hold your breath for a few seconds (only if it feels okay).
- Take slow, deep breaths.
- Sip a little cold water slowly.
- Swallow a small spoon of sugar.
- Breathe into a paper bag for a short time (only with an adult nearby).

Your friend tried to scare you because a sudden shock can sometimes stop the diaphragm’s spasm — but it doesn’t always work, and scaring someone isn’t always nice. If your hiccups last a very long time (more than a few hours) or bother you a lot, tell your parents, grandparents, or your班主任/学校心理老师 so an adult can help.
